That said, 1911s and Glocks are my two favorite to work on. They were designed to be taken apart and put back together by anyone anywhere. The ease of customization is what makes both platforms SO popular.

A CHEAP ($500) 1911 with $250 in GOOD work is a rock solid shooter that will put up with abuse and hold groups with any stock full sized center fire ($1k+ HKs and 1911s included). Add in just a little more for comfort (enhanced controls/sights) they are very hard to beat. The full custom shop guns ($2k+) are made with insane precision and the way they group reflects that.

It is a 110 year old design at it's core, but the nuances, methods, materials have been updated all along. Colt kept the design updated every 10 years (generations) until the 90s when others got in on producing and then the variations on the design have never stopped. You can find 1911s that are classic, even archaic, as well as variations that are still cutting edge.

The defining allure for most people is really down tow just a few things though: The grip is super solid, with a pleasantly rounded front and rear, and a slightly front heavy balance. The look is just iconic, classic, and sexy. The single action trigger comes out of the box on a cheap 1911 better than most competitors at twice the price, and the custom or expertly customized guns are jaw dropping.

Unrelated question, but since you are knowledgeable:

I've generally stuck with 9mm, 40S&W, and 22RL for pistol calibers. Just to keep my life and ammo inventory manageable. (I currently have a couple 'fun' colt 45 caliber guns for the novelty, but not guns I'd spend any time with at the range or hold more than a box or two of ammo for.)

Is there any reason I should move beyond these calibers? If so, what would you recommend? Something in 45 ACP, or 357 or 5.7x28? Or something else?

Not really looking for a new EDC, just wondering what I'm missing.

The short answer is that the reason there are SO many calibers is that they all were designed to fill some niche. The big popular ones that you hear of generally fill their niche fairly well. So what do you want to do with your handgun? If the short answer is "self defense" then the I say, when using the BEST ammunition available today, anything over a .380 is adequate for self defense.

The 9mm is a fair step above that and the cheapest to shoot, hence the mainstream gravity to 9mm. Naturally, bigger calibers with more energy make bigger holes. The 45 has the advantage of diameter over calibers like 38 super and 10mm which certainly have more energy and recoil, but lacking diameter, therefore the wound diameter usually favors the .45 (with a few exceptions in ammunition selection to note) while the penetration of the other two is far beyond the .45 (energy/diameter=penetration [more or less, assuming your bullet holds together and doesn't break apart]). Therefore the 45 is often (begrudgingly) seen as the big boy on the block for self defense against humans, and the calibers with more energy are usually touted for longer distances or dangerous animals.

I want to reiterate that with more energy and the RIGHT ammunition selection the bigger (more energy) calibers can and do make bigger wounds. Here's the rub, given the best ammunition available today in 2020, the 9mm has several choices which will exceed a statistical 95% chance of a "one shot stop". I define this as Evan Marshall did 'one shot to the torso caused the cesation of all aggression and the target traveled no more than six feet from the point they were shot' (from memory).

So as we move up the caliber chain, the .40 breaks over 97%, the 45 over 99%, see where this is going? If you select the very best ammo available the 9mm is reach right up to than 99% mark with a faster return to target than the other two, and the magnum autos (357 Sig, 38 Super, 10mm) are in a different category for a slow return to target.

Now, training is going to overcome shortcomings in both shot placement (more important than wound diameter) and return to target time (less important shot placement). Again with the 9mm being cheapest to train with. . . I'm sure I am beating a dead horse.

I don't think you are MISSING anything, but if you are already using the 40, the biggest appeal to me of that caliber, besides that it's a fantastic short stop on power and capacity, especially in compact autos, is caliber swaps.

In most Smith, Glock, and Sigs, swapping the .40 over to the .357 sig is JUST a $100 barrel swap. BOOM, bottle neck cartridge for better feeding, and better BC for longer distances or more penetration. Again with the 40, $100 barrel, $20 recoil spring, $15 magazine and sometimes a $30 ejector, and you are shooting 9mm out of the same gun.

That's mostly for fun, but the advantage of the .357 or using a 9mm in a 40 slide/frame is the thicker heavier barrel, and heavier slide (compared to 9mm) mean you get smoother recoil and less muzzle flip. With Glock in particular, which dominates the 9mm market, and only offers their Gen5 in 9mm (they make a REALLY good 9mm) I would only have a 9mm if I got a 40 and converted for that difference in recoil, unless I just HAD to have the Gen5 which, being beefier than the Gen4 has lighter recoil anyway, but still more than one of my conversions.

So after all of that rambling. You have a 9 and 40. Those are more than adequate for self defense at 30 feet or less. If you need to stop a dangerous animal or reach out to well beyond 30' the penetration or margin for error on shot placement begins to become very attractive.

A good (and that part is important) 1911 is a pleasure to shoot. The trigger pull is light, short, and crisp, the weight of the pistol soaks up a good deal of the recoil, it leaves a nice, big hole, and it fits the hand beautifully. I own a 1911, I carried it concealed for years, and if you asked me what my favorite pistol to shoot is, I would say it's a 1911.

However, they're heavy, the design came about when labor was cheap and technology was expensive (the opposite of what exists now), innovations in materials and designs have created lighter, more reliable pistols that require virtually no hand-fitting, and bullet design, especially as it relates to hollowpoints, is light-years ahead of where it was even 30 years ago. Now, a 9mm with quality JHP rounds offers virtually identical terminal ballistics as the same company and brand's .45 ACP JHP rounds. A Glock 19 costs a tenth what a good 1911 runs, weighs half as much, holds twice as much ammo, and parts replacement requires little more than a pulse.

Still, a good / tuned 1911 is thing of beauty, but nowadays, they're mostly barbecue guns, built for competition, or more a pistol of station than duty.
